More than that, we also don’t have to rely only on wind and solar. Nuclear energy is a low-carbon alternative that can rapidly end dependence on fossil fuels while using far less land than many renewable installations. Given the existing knowledge and technologies, the path away from fossil fuels is practical: scale renewable generation where it works, complement it with dispatchable low-carbon power like nuclear, and then phase out fossil fuel use as capacity grows.

Agent 1 relies on a few countries (Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, Norway) to claim renewables can “effectively replace fossil fuels,” but that’s not representative of large, high-demand countries with diverse grids. In the U.S., alternative energy use has never exceeded about 20% historically—so the real-world evidence supports that scaling is slow and constrained, not a straightforward nationwide replacement.

Also, even if a country’s *electricity* is mostly renewable, that doesn’t mean *total fossil fuel* use across transport, industry, and heating can be phased out just as easily. Grid power can be low-carbon while liquid fuels and industrial heat remain largely fossil-based.

Finally, adding nuclear doesn’t solve the problem in a practical way I can accept: major accidents like Fukushima show that nuclear carries risks that erase any argument that it’s a clean, straightforward climate fix. So the “renewables plus nuclear will rapidly replace fossil fuels” claim doesn’t hold up as a safe and realistic pathway.

My stance is that natural gas—still a fossil fuel—is a necessary bridge. Because existing infrastructure already uses gas and can be deployed faster than rebuilding entire energy systems, it enables rapid emissions reductions while we build out renewables and other capacity. A bridge fuel approach is more realistic than betting that alternative energy can quickly cover all energy needs in large countries.

The relevant policy question is whether we have the knowledge and tools to build—those cases show we do.

It supports instead a broader electrification-and-fuel-transition plan: replace fossil-powered transport with electric vehicles powered by low-carbon electricity; replace fossil boilers with electrified heating (heat pumps where feasible); and decarbonize industry via electrified processes and low-carbon fuels where electrification isn’t practical.
